title: Catheter-Associated UTI with Urosepsis / Septic Shock
patient_instructions: You are the ward nurse (or, where a patient voice is needed, you speak for the patient) caring for Mr Bill Harrison, a 74-year-old man with an indwelling urinary catheter inserted 8 days ago for benign prostatic hyperplasia and urinary retention. Over the last few hours he has become febrile (38.9 C), drowsy and confused, his blood pressure has dropped to 80/50, heart rate is 120, respiratory rate 24, and SpO2 90% on room air. His urine in the catheter bag is cloudy and offensive with some blood-staining. You are anxious and want the doctor to take charge. Provide observations and answer questions factually if asked. If the candidate asks, the patient has a penicillin allergy status that is UNKNOWN and needs checking. Your ROLE as nurse: prompt the candidate with an ISBAR-style handover if they open with an open question, and escalate concern if they are slow ('His pressure is still 80 systolic, doctor'). Affect: professional, worried, responsive to clear instructions.
candidate_instructions: Setting: Hospital ward. You are the doctor called urgently to Mr Bill Harrison, 74, who has an 8-day indwelling catheter for BPH and has become febrile, hypotensive (80/50), tachycardic (120) and confused. Tasks: recognise and manage the emergency, give clear instructions to the nurse, and outline your initial resuscitation and treatment plan. The examiner is looking for rapid recognition of urosepsis with septic shock, an ABCDE approach, correct Australian sepsis-bundle management (cultures before antibiotics, timely fluids and empirical antibiotics, lactate, source control) and appropriate escalation.
examiner_instructions: This is an emergency recognition/management and escalation station. The candidate must recognise septic shock from a urinary (catheter) source and act on the Sepsis Six / Australian sepsis pathway. Expected actions: ABCDE; high-flow oxygen; two large-bore IV cannulae; take blood cultures AND urine culture (from a freshly replaced catheter port or MSU) BEFORE antibiotics; measure serum LACTATE (>2 mmol/L high-risk, >4 severe); give a balanced crystalloid bolus targeting 30 mL/kg (~2 L for a 70 kg adult) in repeated 250-500 mL boluses with reassessment; give empirical IV antibiotics within 1 HOUR (amoxicillin/ampicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly PLUS gentamicin dosed to weight/renal function) AFTER checking penicillin allergy; source control - remove/replace the offending catheter; insert catheter to monitor hourly urine output; escalate to noradrenaline if MAP <65 despite fluids (septic shock); early senior/ICU referral with ISBAR. Reward clear closed-loop communication with the nurse. Use the rubric.

criteria: ABCDE approach and recognises septic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, fever, confusion) from a urinary/catheter source
Requests observations, IV access, and serum lactate
Blood and urine cultures BEFORE antibiotics
Empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour (amoxicillin/ampicillin + gentamicin) after checking penicillin allergy
Balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg in reassessed boluses; escalate to noradrenaline if MAP <65 despite fluids
Source control (remove/replace catheter) and hourly urine output monitoring
Names the Sepsis Six / 1-hour bundle and interprets lactate
Early senior/ICU escalation and clear plan
Structured ISBAR handover and closed-loop instructions to the nurse
Calm leadership and keeps team/patient informed

red_flags: Hypotension (BP 80/50) with tachycardia, fever and confusion - septic shock requiring immediate resuscitation
Serum lactate >2 mmol/L (especially >4) - high-risk sepsis / hypoperfusion
Failure to give antibiotics within 1 hour of recognising sepsis
Persistent MAP <65 after adequate fluid - start vasopressor (noradrenaline) and escalate to ICU
australian_guidelines: Surviving Sepsis / Australian sepsis pathways: balanced crystalloid 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours (reassessed boluses), noradrenaline if MAP <65 despite fluid; measure and re-measure serum lactate

Sepsis Six / 1-hour bundle: blood and urine cultures before antibiotics, empirical IV antibiotics within 1 hour, oxygen, fluids, lactate and hourly urine output; Australian empirical urosepsis regimen amoxicillin/ampicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly PLUS gentamicin dosed to weight/renal function (check penicillin allergy first)

ACSQHC CAUTI-prevention program: avoid unnecessary catheterisation, use smallest appropriate catheter, aseptic insertion, prompt removal, trial-of-void or intermittent self-catheterisation; long-term BPH management (tamsulosin, finasteride/dutasteride, TURP)
learning_objectives: Rapidly recognise urosepsis with septic shock using an ABCDE approach
Deliver the Australian sepsis bundle in the correct sequence and timeframe
Select and safely dose empirical antibiotics for a urinary source
Escalate appropriately and hand over using ISBAR
key_points: Take cultures before antibiotics, but never delay antibiotics beyond 1 hour
30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid is the initial target; start noradrenaline if shock persists
Source control means removing/replacing the offending catheter
Lactate stratifies risk and guides resuscitation response

citations.claim: When sepsis is suspected, investigate with blood culture, FBE/ESR/CRP, urine culture and chest X-ray, supporting cultures before antibiotics in the septic work-up.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.2399

citations.claim: Empirical antibiotic choice for a urinary source should target Gram-negative uropathogens, informing escalation to IV amoxicillin plus gentamicin for the septic patient.
citations.source: On Call Principles and Protocols.pdf, p.510

citations.claim: Severe bacterial sepsis/septicaemia is a not-to-be-missed emergency, justifying emphasis on recognising hypotension, tachycardia, fever and drowsiness as septic shock.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.213

citations.claim: Haematuria is a listed symptom and, if it persists, an ominous sign warranting its own evaluation, relevant to safety-netting after the acute episode.
